author: Thaer Abu Aoun, Omar Moussa
title: Israel expands occupied zone in Gaza City’s Zeitoun, orders evacuations in Deir al-Balah
content:
Israel extended the area under its control along Gaza’s eastern edge earlier this week, carrying out military operations in Gaza City and Deir al-Balah that forced people into displacement, eyewitnesses in both cities told Mada Masr.


The two governorates lie adjacent to the “yellow line” established under the October ceasefire agreement, marking the zone that has remained under Israeli occupation. In recent months, Israeli forces have gradually pushed beyond that line, issuing evacuation orders farther west ahead of military advances.


In Gaza City’s southeastern Zeitoun neighborhood, the Israeli military began operations on Saturday with heavy artillery shelling that forced dozens of families to flee westward, an eyewitness who lives in the neighborhood told Mada Masr.


Military vehicles then advanced into eastern Zeitoun as far as Salah Eddin Road, bringing the Dawla and Mostawsaf areas within the occupied zone.


After forcing residents to leave, the military “immediately began targeting anyone entering the area,” the eyewitness said.


Two residents of Zeitoun said shelling continued over the next two days, driving further displacement. Early Sunday, three people were killed and several others injured when Israeli shelling hit a gathering of civilians on Kashko Street near the Dawla junction in southern Zeitoun, the residents told Mada Masr.


Further south in central Gaza, Israeli forces ordered residents of Deir al-Balah’s Um Dhahir neighborhood to evacuate immediately on Saturday, a resident told Mada Masr. Later that night and into the early hours of Sunday morning, airstrikes hit around 12 homes, forcing out nearly 70 families and people who had taken refuge there after earlier displacement.


The advances in Zeitoun continue a months-long expansion of Israeli control along Gaza’s eastern edge. Under the first phase of the ceasefire agreement, Israeli forces were expected to withdraw and remain within a designated zone, which covers around 53 percent of the strip. But they have instead continued to expand beyond it. Aid workers

told

 Reuters that Israeli military maps distributed to aid agencies in March showed the creation of a new “orange line” that increased the area under Israeli control by around 11 percent of Gaza’s territory.


Israeli-backed militias have

carried

out raids within this new zone, forcing people out of their homes ahead of military advances.

The post

Israel expands occupied zone in Gaza City’s Zeitoun, orders evacuations in Deir al-Balah

 first appeared on

Mada Masr

.

author: Unknown
title: Luis Olvera Maldonado - (Excerpts from) The Social Revolution in Northern Mexico and the Anarchist Communes of the Mexican Liberal Party 1911–1915
content:
“If, from the beginning, we had called ourselves anarchists, nobody save for a few would’ve listened to us. Without calling ourselves anarchists we’ve been lighting up in the minds ideas of hatred against the propertied class and against the governmental caste.”

–Ricardo Flores Magón, Letter to Enrique Flores Magón and Práxedis G. Guerrero, June 13, 1908

Mexico inaugurated the 20th Century with revolution, igniting a spark that would go on to engulf the rest of history throughout the world. The spark had been set in the 1906 miner’s strike in Cananea, veterans of the strike such as Fernando Palomarez, Pedro Ramírez Cuale, José Mariá Leyva, would go on to take the incendiary actions and lessons learned then and harness them into full-blown rebellion under the guidance of the brothers Ricardo and Enrique Flores Magón. Their project, one of nominally liberal reform against Porfirio Díaz, belied the true anti-governmental and anti-capitalist stance taken by the central Board of the party; as Malatesta once said, “... we must, in certain conditions, avoid mentioning socialism and anarchy, but only as long as our practice is socialism and anarchy. We may well not speak out against the government, but only as long as we are actually attacking the government; we can steer clear of talk directed against property, but only as long as our practice is expropriation.”[1] No one had learned this better than the members of el Partido Liberal Mexicano, the Mexican Liberal Party.

More than any other faction that partook in the Mexican Revolution, theirs was the most far-sighted and radical of them all. They were aided in solidarity by many then and now renown figures such as Jack London and Eugene Debs though the backbone of their movement was comprised by members of the IWW and other American anarchists such Big Bill Haywood, Joe Hill, Alexander Berkman, Emma Goldman, Voltairine de Cleyre, and Pyotr Kropotkin among many, many other lesser known but nonetheless just as important figures to the movement.

Reader, you hold the collective effort to preserve a long overlooked part of socialist history that was the Partido Liberal Mexicano that set itself to gather all of its forces to see through a social revolution, an economic revolution —an anarchist revolution. In these pages you will find some of the first-ever translated documents gathered by comrade Maldonado that means to give a chronology of the PLM revolution, its trajectory narrated by both its adherents and opponents in their own words. The importance of these can’t be overstated, nor can the contributions of the anarchists at the time minimized, the world would go on soon to feel the economic-political pressures the Mexicans did, and follow suit in their own manner; had they learned the lessons of the dangers of a simply political, governmental revolution, would the Russian and Spanish revolutions played out differently? As haunting as that question may hang over our heads, it is all the more reason for us to learn.

It is no small feat that they managed to mobilize both people from as far as Wales and Russia but also African-Americans and Indigenous Cupapá and Mayo Indians, all experimenting with what a world outside of State and Capital may look like. More than any revolution before them, they tapped into a solidarity rarely seen or imitated to the degree of sincerity that was shown in those short years of revolutionary upheaval.

The brothers Flores Magón are usually forgotten when talking about the Mexican Revolution since they have to share the stage with impressive and romantic figures such as Pancho Villa and Emiliano Zapata, their fellow revolutionaries on the front lines and yet it must be remarked that their struggle lives on to this day; a section of the EZLN is named after them and the watchword Tierra y Libertad, “Land and Liberty” was introduced by PLM to later be taken up by Zapata.

We hope these short snippets, presented here, showcase the continuation of the webs of mutual aid first established all those years ago during the glorious days of revolution for more than a hundred years now. A forthcoming full translation of the work is in the works and if there’s something to be mourned it is the lack of attention paid to the female anarchists of the day; something that was remedied by comrade Maldonado’s second book in this series, Revolucionarias, rebeldes, y anarquistas: Las mujeres en el Partido Liberal Mexicano, “Revolutionaries, Rebels and Anarchists …

Empire is materializing before our very eyes. Over the past several decades, as colonial regimes were overthrown and then precipitously after the Soviet barriers to the capitalist world market finally collapsed, we have witnessed an irresistible and irreversible globalization of economic and cultural exchanges. Along with the global market and global circuits of production has emerged a global order, a new logic and structure of rule—in short, a new form of sovereignty. Empire is the political subject that effectively regulates these global exchanges, the sovereign power that governs the world.

Many argue that the globalization of capitalist production and exchange means that economic relations have become more autonomous from political controls, and consequently that political sovereignty has declined. Some celebrate this new era as the liberation of the capitalist economy from the restrictions and distortions that political forces have imposed on it; others lament it as the closing of the institutional channels through which workers and citizens can influence or contest the cold logic of capitalist profit. It is certainly true that, in step with the processes of globalization, the sovereignty of nation-states, while still effective, has progressively declined. The primary factors of production and exchange— money, technology, people, and goods—move with increasing ease across national boundaries; hence the nation-state has less and less power to regulate these flows and impose its authority over the economy. My mother, Santosh Sharma, died while I was working on this book. In many ways I’ve written it because of—and for—her. Like so many of us, she was continuously refashioned according to the historical changes taking place in state forms, and through an ever-encompassing capitalism. My mother was born a “British subject.” As the clock ticked past midnight on the day India achieved home rule, she was made an “Indian national.” That same day, she set out for the Delhi railway station to bring food to those forced to flee Pakistan, the other side of partitioned British India. There she encountered people desperate to flee massacres in India and she offered them food as well. Santosh lived the second half of her life in Vancouver, first as an “immigrant” and then as a “Canadian citizen.”

Denigrated as a “native” in British India, Santosh and her parents strongly supported M. K. Gandhi’s nationalist version of decolonization. My father, Kesho Ram Sharma, was a communist and held a different view of decolonization than my mother, but he was enthralled with modernity. Kesho took Santosh to see her first film: Mother India, a classic tale of development. He also forced her to have three abortions in order to comply with India’s modernization campaign of two children per (nuclear) family. When my parents immigrated to Canada with my brother and me, we were among the first cohort admitted after Canada’s “preferred races and nations” clause was removed. title: Michael Taylor - Introduction to ‘The Possibility of Cooperation’
content:
The problem of collective action

Solutions? Community, states, entrepreneurs, property rights and norms

The most persuasive justification of the state is founded on the argument that, without it, people would not successfully cooperate in realizing their common interests and in particular would not provide themselves with certain public goods : goods, that is to say, which any member of the public may benefit from, whether or not he or she contributes in any way to their provision. The most appealing version of this justification would confine the argument about voluntary cooperation to what are supposed to be the most fundamental public goods: goods (or services) which are thought to be preconditions of the pursuit and attainment of all other valued ends, including less basic public goods, and are therefore desired by everyone within the jurisdiction of the state in question.

The Possibility of Cooperation is a critique of this justification of the state, and the heart of the critique (chapters 2 4 below) is a detailed study of cooperation in the absence of the state and of other kinds of coercion. (The arguments about public goods provision and the theory of cooperation which make up these chapters can be read — and assessed — independently of the critique of the Hobbesian justification of the state.)

Hobbes’s Leviathan was the first full expression of this way of justifying the state. The public goods with which he was principally concerned were social order — domestic peace and security — and defence against foreign aggression. Without these, very little else that was worth having could be had. Without internal and external security, there would be not only actual violence but such pervasive uncertainty as to undermine the incentive to invest resources in any projects with delayed returns. But although everyone would prefer the condition of peace and security that mutual restraint ensures to the ‘war of all against all’ that is the result of everyone pursuing his own interests without restraint, no individual has the incentive, in the absence of the state, to restrain himself. It is therefore rational, says Hobbes, for everyone to institute a government with sufficient power to ensure that everybody keeps the peace.[1]

Many writers who came after Hobbes, including some who professed no sympathy with what they took to be Hobbes’s ideas, have taken over the core of his case for the state. Most economists who nowadays write about public goods believe that the failure of people to provide themselves voluntarily with these goods constitutes at least a prima facie case for state activity, and most of them presume that the state is the only means for remedying this failure.[2] (For nearly all the rest, the remedy is to establish or extend private property rights. I’ll comment briefly on this view later in the chapter.)

Of course, many people believe that the state can be justified on further grounds and that it has functions other than that of providing public goods. Certainly, modern states do more than provide such goods. Hov/ever, the justification I wish to criticize here is common to the arguments of nearly all those who believe that the state is necessary. Its persuasiveness lies in the fact that the state, on this view, exists to further common interests, to do what everybody wants done. Other arguments — for example, that income redistribution is desirable and can be brought about only through the intervention of the state — do not appeal to common interests, not, at any rate, in an obvious or uncontroversial way.

In recent years, this argument about the necessity of the state has found new supporters amongst those concerned with the degradation of the environment, the depletion of non-renewable resources and rapid population growth. According to them, people will not voluntarily refrain from discharging untreated wastes into rivers and lakes, from hunting whales and other species threatened with extinction, from having ‘too many children’, and so on. Only powerful state action, they say. can solve or avert these problems, which are the consequence of failures to provide public goods (and more generally ‘non-excludable’ goods about which more later). For many environmentalists, some of these public goods are at least as fundamental as peace and security were for Hobbes. Continued failure to provide them will eventually result in ecological catastrophe. Without them, the life of man will not just be …

“In writing an overview of both anarcho-nihilist thought and concentration camp resistance, I have omitted much. The nihilist themes of negation, time, and organization could have happily been joined by conversations about identity abolishment, queerness, domestication, and more. Stories of Häftlinge who lashed back against the camp systems could have been elaborated by countless stories of escape, mutual aid, and nonviolent civil disobedience, all of which played a part in the broader story of resistance in the Lagers. There are many questions and topics that still remain unexplored for me.”

Serafinski, Afterthought from Blessed is the Flame

A few months ago a comrade & I decided to take on the task of creating a condensed version of Blessed is the Flame. This was in response to a vast misunderstanding & fash jacketing of those who post content on nihilist thought.

This task turned out to be more difficult than we imagined. Condensing 50+ pages wasn’t easy, at times it felt wrong to even omit some of the passages/stories from the book. On a particular night of working on this project the question came up of whether or not this was a disservice to all the people who’s stories were told in the book. But we found solace in the ‘Afterthoughts’.

There will never be enough paper to document all the stories of those who were imprisoned in the camps. Many of them are still relatively unknown & majority of the ones that are, ended in tragedy. Most of the prisoners who resisted were met with swift death. So knowing all the tragedy and suffering that happened — how did this book become so important to us?

Enough for us to spend months trying to compile a shorter read for people to have access to?

Blessed was our introduction to nihilist resistance. On a summer morning in the middle of the desert it became a sacred text to us. We poured over the pages, read & re read each section — the stories lit a fire under us. When you pick this up its our hope that you may be consumed by that same fire.

“I find it comforting that everything is so hopeless”

We are being led to our slaughter. This has been theorized in a thousand ways, described in environmental, social, and political terms, it has been prophesied, abstracted, and narrated in real time, and still we are unsure of what to do with it. The underlying point is that the progressity of society has nothing to offer us and everything to take away. Often it feels like we are giving it away without a fight: when we sell our time for money, allow our passions to be commodified, invest ourselves in the betterment of society, or sustain ourselves on the spoils of ecological destruction, we openly (though not consensually) participate in our own destruction.

The question hangs in an ethereal and ghastly voice: Why do you let yourselves be led to the slaughter like sheep?

Underneath the ubiquitous sheep-to-the-slaughter metaphor is buried a profound historical possibility: wherever the Nazis sought to impose domination and violence, people resisted. Behind the images of people wearing armbands, boarding trains, and walking placidly into gas chambers, lies a rich history of recalcitrance’ and insurrection.

A different approach: We have already been led to our slaughter — it is all around us. The world in which we exist is a protracted death, a sort of economically-sustained limbo in which hearts are permitted to beat only to the extent that they can facilitate the upward stream of capital. The plague of domestication has reached into every wild space, and the lines of colonization have crossed us more times than we can count. Every unproductive aspect of the biosphere has been flagged for eradication, from the “beam-trawled ocean floors” to the “dynamited reefs” to the “hollowed-out mountains,”’ the highest calibers of technology are locked into a perpetual killing spree chugging along In a “monotonous rhythm of death.” We who still have air in our lungs are the living dead, and struggle daily to remember what it feels like to be alive, holding tightly to the “desire for wildness that the misery of a paycheck cannot allay.” We roam the desolate architecture of our slaughter houses (“the prison of civilization we live in”) like ghosts who feel but cannot quite understand …

author: Unknown
title: Sasha Warren - Open propositions for a strategic madness
content:
1. Madness is itself a strategy.

2. Strategies can appear as madness.

3. Sanity, feigned or “real,” is also a strategy.

4. On the one hand, we face the threat of non-being; on the other, the threat of having to be.

5. Psychiatry is a strategic assemblage.

6. The character of resistance corresponds to the contradiction in question, and can deepen it or resolve it by other means.

7. There is much to destroy, but this entails neither a celebration of violence nor its naive denunciation.

8. Take heart: we are compromised and impure in madness

“Though this be madness, yet there is method in’t.” –William Shakespeare, Hamlet.

These propositions are intended neither as statements of fact about the state of things nor as prescriptions for budding radicals and activists, but merely as distilled reflections, as questions, and as provocations.

This bit of wisdom is as old as the concept of madness itself. In the Phaedrus, Socrates remunerates forms of beneficial, necessary madness: the manic art of prophecy, the Bacchic swell of poetry, and refuge or “relief from the greatest plagues of trouble” (244c-e). What are the madnesses in I Never Promised You a Rose Garden by Joanne Greenberg, A Question of Power by Bessie Head, or any of the stories by Anna Kavan besides trips along unpaved, densely wooded pathways to a new life and an escape from the old horrors? In mystic tours through inner Hell and the nest of unreason that shelters from the Hell without alike, madness is best understood as a strategic event. Even some psychiatrists and psychoanalysis know this. Freud, in his text on Schreber, wrote that “delusion-formation, which we take to be a pathological product, is in reality an attempt at recovery, a process of reconstruction” (147). R.D. Laing recognized the same: “without exception the experience and behavior that gets labelled schizophrenic is a special strategy that the person invents in order to live in an unlivable situation” (95). Mad strategies are methods of survival and healing. The poet Jody Chan has picked up on this theme quite explicitly in a new poem called “Madness is a Strategy.” They remind us that sometimes madness is warranted as an explosion of rage, or even needed as a “structure of possibility” which “can force us to build bonds that outlast periods of crisis, political projects, the constrictions of capitalism.” To view madness in this way is not to reduce the experience of insanity or mental illness to a matter of conscious choice for the mad person nor to call it a happy choice. We do not often get to choose the strategies that sustain us, and it is a common occurrence that one must make sacrifices in order to survive the game.

It can happen that what is called madness is a pathologization of resistant acts. Here, madness is a distorted reflection of militant strategies, which are pathologized. This is notoriously common in revolutionary situations and anti-colonial wars. During the Paris Commune, Briere de Boismont wrote:

There are still fanatics who dream of remaking the world through workable schemes, these being the first elements of demagogic insanity; but there is above all a multitude of individuals who hold ideas about the family, property, individual freedom, intelligence, and the constitution of society that are so opposed to human nature that madness alone can explain them. (In Murat, 216)

Fanon’s psychiatric work lingers on the undecidability that comes with trying to recognize madness within a colonial system of immense, daily violence and degradation combined with the colonial administration’s desire to diminish the legitimacy of resistance by characterizing it as the expression of the mentally disturbed. Colonial psychiatry is tasked with naturalizing the racial inferiority of the colonized, on the one hand, and pathologizing the toxic effect it has on their bodies and minds (See: Warren, “Healing”). But we cannot simply say that this is a matter of misapprehension, either, for madness expresses a position in relation to sanity. It often happens that the person most assured of their own sanity is believed to be mad by the world without; there is no true or just mechanism for deciding this once and for all. Bonaventure Ndikung reminds us that sanity and sanitation are related through the Latin root sanus (28): sanity is what results when the social world has been sanitized, cleaned of corrupting influence. Insofar as the colonial administration represents sanity and …

title: French Polynesia objects to an American seabed mining plan made without its input
content:
The government of French Polynesia plans to challenge an American startup’s proposal to explore the waters just beyond its maritime borders for seabed mining. 


“We were approached, but we were not consulted,” Moetai Brotherson, the territory’s president, told Grist. “We are not remaining passive while industrial activities are proposed immediately next to ecosystems that French Polynesia has chosen to protect.”


As Grist reported last week,

a Bay Area investor wants the Trump administration’s approval

 to explore seabed mining in international waters entirely surrounded by the maritime borders of the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia. The company, American Deep Sea Minerals, has a permit application pending before U.S. regulators and hopes to extract minerals essential to the production of batteries and military technologies. It is one of at least a dozen applications under consideration as President Trump races to make the United States a leader in critical mineral mining. 


Negotiators from dozens of countries are meeting this month in Jamaica at the headquarters of the International Seabed Authority, where they are debating the minutiae of a regulatory framework that’s been in progress for more than a decade. Last year, the Trump administration invited companies to apply for permits to mine the high seas directly through the U.S. rather than wait for the adoption of those rules. That has prompted global outrage from countries who say it flouts international law. 


“The deep seabed belongs to no single country and no corporation; it belongs to all of us,” Letitia Carvalho, the secretary-general of the regulatory body,

said in Jamaica

 last week. “If we lose sight of this, we risk repeating on the ocean floor the same injustices and destruction we still strive to remedy on land.” 


French Polynesia doesn’t have a seat at the authority because it remains a French territory whose Indigenous people haven’t been granted political self-determination. And until recently, when environmental nonprofit organizations extended their observer status to Indigenous advocates, the voices of French Polynesians were largely left out of the discussion. Still, Brotherson said he prefers the international regulatory process to recent U.S. actions. 


“This case therefore goes beyond one company or one licence application,” Brotherson said. It raises a fundamental question, he said, about whether an individual country can unilaterally authorize a new industry in international waters, particularly those adjacent to Pacific island nations and protected marine areas. 


According to Brotherson, American Deep Sea Minerals sent a brief introductory email to a government representative; the government replied asking for more information. “No response was received,” he said. “Thus, no consultation has taken place regarding this proposal, and the government has not been provided with sufficient information to assess the project or its potential environmental implications.” Under international law, Indigenous peoples have the

right to free, prior and informed consent

 — and to withhold such consent — regarding development and extractive projects on their ancestral territories. 


Graham Goulet, the CEO of American Metals, told Grist the company intended to consult the governments of the Cook Islands, Kiribati, and French Polynesia “as the exploration program develops.” Those discussions will, he said, occur under U.S. oversight and in accordance with the intentions outlined in its application. The filing notes that it intends to create a benefit sharing agreement with Pacific nations and plans to avoid interfering with fishing.


The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, the U.S. government agency overseeing seabed licenses in international waters, is still considering Goulet’s application. It is available for public comment

online until August 3

.

Indigenous concerns surface as Trump calls for seabed mining in Alaskan waters


Anita Hofschneider


The environmental implications of seabed mining have long concerned French Polynesia, which banned the practice in 2022, followed quickly by France in 2023. Indigenous peoples with longstanding connections to the ocean, such as for

traditional navigation

, account for 80 percent of the territory’s population. Studies show extraction could harm fisheries, and Indigenous Pasifika leaders from across the region have

raised cultural concerns

author: Amira El-Fekki
title: Sayed Moshagheb trial over homecoming celebration postponed by terrorism court
content:
A Cairo special terrorism court postponed on Monday the trial of former Ultras White Knights leader Sayed Fahim, known as Sayed Moshagheb, and five others to September 22.  


The session was the first in the case against Moshagheb and his friends, who are facing charges of unlawful assembly and possession of fireworks over a gathering they held to celebrate his release after nearly 11 years in detention.


The defense team submitted several procedural requests before the court, including hearing witnesses and presenting evidence, defense lawyer Osama al-Gohary told Mada Masr.


Moshagheb was released on April 16 after spending over a decade detained in connection with the 2015 Air Defense Stadium case and a subsequent case with the State Security Prosecution. 


Hours after his release, following a spontaneous gathering organized by friends outside his home in Bulaq al-Dakrour, he and five others were

rearrested

.


The Interior Ministry had

described

 the celebration of Moshagheb’s release as a “riot,” where fireworks were launched and traffic was disrupted in the Giza neighborhood, “causing public alarm.” 


The lawyer challenged official police and investigation reports which claimed the six were “caught in the act” on the street shortly after Moshagheb arrived in his neighborhood, saying that he was taken from inside his house after the gathering that was held for him.


In a Friday

statement

, the Ultras White Knights described Moshagheb’s April arrest as a “moment of hope turned into shock,” stating that there had been no violence or misconduct that justified escalation on behalf of authorities. 


Moshagheb was a founding

member

 of the Ultras White Knights, the football fan group of Egypt’s Zamalek Club that became politically engaged in the years after the 2011 uprising. He has a long history with the state crackdown that followed the military’s ouster of former President Mohamed Morsi in 2013, as authorities targeted young activists, students and groups, including football ultras. 


Now 36, he was

arrested

 in 2015 in the wake of the Air Defense Stadium case, where security forces fired tear gas at fans outside the over-crowded stadium, causing a stampede that killed 20 people. In 2017, he received a seven-year sentence for possession of explosives, vandalism of public facilities and assault against security forces. 


New charges against Moshagheb were brought against him by the State Security Prosecution in 2021, including joining an illegal group and spreading false news, keeping him behind bars, according five human rights organizations, who condemned in a

joint statement

 authorities’ “

continued policy of not releasing political detainees after the end of their prison term or after dropping charges against them

.” 


His continued imprisonment is part of what has become known as the state’s “recycling” of political detainees, a practice human rights lawyers say has

increased

 over past years. According to his lawyer, he had been accused in 13 cases before the April release order.

Sayed Moshagheb trial over homecoming celebration postponed by terrorism court

Mada Masr

author: Dionne Phillips
title: As climate change threatens their lands, Indigenous nations demand more power at the UN
content:
This story is published through the Indigenous News Alliance.


The Arctic is warming four times faster than other regions, a trend that disproportionately harms the Indigenous Sámi people — particularly their access to vital traditional resources like reindeer and salmon, which are used for food, clothing, weapons, and more.


As northern temperatures rise, snow is melting and refreezing at an accelerating rate. That forms ice, preventing reindeer from reaching the lichen below and dramatically increasing

starvation rates

. “Those impacts in nature are severe for our culture and livelihoods,” said Tuomas Aslak Juuso, vice president of the

Sámediggi

, or Sámi Parliament, of Finland. “So survival of reindeer and then survival of our livelihoods [and] cultures is then questioned.” 


Last week, the impacts of climate change and colonialism were among the key issues raised by the hundreds of Indigenous people gathered in Geneva. They’d come from around the world to discuss these mounting threats at the United Nations Expert Mechanism on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, or EMRIP. They agreed that a multitude of crises will only grow worse unless they are given greater say in international negotiations and decision-making. That’s why in addition to pushing specific policy recommendations on conflict, AI, and other key issues, Indigenous delegates continued their decades-long demand for better representation at the U.N.


“What we are trying to do is to get some implementation resources for us to adapt to the climate change. With Finland, for example, we don’t have any adaptation resources on how to adapt to these situations,” Juuso said. “To be able to bring these issues forward to the global discussion, we would have to have the opportunity to participate.”


Member states are granted access to U.N. gatherings, where they can easily express views, determine policies, and outline their progress implementing international commitments required by the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples and other agreements. But Indigenous advocates say the voices of the peoples directly impacted by such actions aren’t always heard at international forums. 


The U.N. structure requires participation through either a member state or a registered civil society agency — for instance, a non-governmental organization, academic institution, or accredited Indigenous organization. But Indigenous nations don’t fit neatly into one of those categories and are reduced to participating as NGOs. Beyond those structural barriers, Indigenous peoples also face financial and other resource challenges that compound the difficulty of making themselves heard at the international level. That’s why those attending EMRIP continued the long fight for what is called enhanced participation, which could finally give Indigenous nations and organizations the same access and power the United States and other countries enjoy.


That increased influence is especially important when many countries ignore Indigenous priorities. Throughout the week, many delegates identified climate and environmental issues as one area where national governments often have different priorities than Indigenous peoples, who consider land and ecosystems more important than economic growth — a value system they believe is at odds with the world’s best interests. 


Read Next


For Indigenous peoples, conflict means so much more than war


Te Aniwaniwa Paterson


“We’ve got to try and balance immediate economic interests with longer-term environmental protections,” said Kym Hamilton, who is from the tribes of Ngāti Kahungunu, Ngā Rauru, Ngāti Raukawa in Aotearoa New Zealand. “I think we’ve got a responsibility to protect our descendants.”


In U.N. lexicon,

enhanced participation

 is the catchphrase often used for efforts to elevate Indigenous peoples’ voices. Those gathered in Geneva asserted the right to represent their communities in crucial global discussions that impact them. They are also demanding more respect from member-state governments and other policymakers, something they argue will better help them to survive conflict and other crises.


“The question before us is no longer whether Indigenous peoples should participate more fully in the Human Rights Council,” Hamilton, who spoke on behalf of the National Iwi Chairs Forum that represents 87 tribes, said. “The question now is how quickly we will implement these commitments.”

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Behind bars, political prisoners assert freedom
content:
MANILA – Behind bars, political prisoners found a way to document their lives, struggles, and aspirations. 


This book entitled, “Pansamantalang Mundo” (Temporary World) was launched on Saturday, July 18, alongside the launch of LAYA, a national and international campaign calling for the immediate release of political prisoners in the Philippines.  


 “Recorded in this book is the free thought, feeling, and creativity of political prisoners whom the state has tried to silence,” said Chingbee Cruz of Paper Trail Projects, the publisher of the book, in Filipino. “This book is a firm refusal to the state’s deliberate erasure of a reasoned action in pursuit of a just society.”


“Pansamantalang Mundo” book published by Paper Trail Projects, in partnership with Karapatan. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.


The book is a product of almost two years of jail visits and writing workshops at the Correctional Institute for Women (CIW), compiling all of their works. The learning has been reciprocal: the publishers also learned about the conditions not only of political prisoners but of other persons deprived of liberty (PDL) inside the facility.


“We learned so much, including the daily indignities they experienced. Due to lack of spaces and beds, the floor and hallways become the sleeping quarters for those in detention. When even a passageway is designated as a resting place, even sleep and rest are denied to those stripped of their freedom,” Cruz added.


July 18 also marks the

Nelson Mandela International Day

, observed in honor of Nelson Mandela, South Africa’s first black president, whose legacy is rooted in the fight for human rights, equality and social justice. The

UN adopted in December 2015

the Nelson Mandela Rules or the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners. It is considered the global blueprint for safe, secure, and humane prison management. 


“Imprisonment only takes away a person’s physical freedom,” Cruz recalled the words of CIW political prisoners in Filipino. “But it cannot take away the freedom to think, to feel, to speak, to write stories, and to create images that represent what the heart truly feels and what the mind imagines.”


In the Philippines alone, the jail congestion is a problem in ensuring a dignified living for persons deprived of liberty (PDLs). At present, the national congestion rate of facilities supervised and managed by the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) is at 294 percent. 


Karapatan recorded 560 total number of political prisoners, with 165 arrested under the administration of Ferdinand Marcos Jr.


Symbolic paper cranes were attached in a steel frame, holding the calls for the freedom of all political prisoners. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.


Marilyn Magpatoc, a political prisoner for 11 years and one of the authors of the book, hoped that the book will serve as an inspiration and a space to think for those who will read it. She read an excerpt, a poem she wrote while she was still in detention.


“Sa tinin ng kaaway sila’y nagwagi / Na ang diwa ko’y kanilang nagapi / Araw-araw pinapatunayan kong sila’y mali / Diwang aktibista’y di kailanman mababali,” Magpatoc recited.


Former political prisoner Amanda Echanis, LAYA spokesperson, emphasized that the people in power and those who are also implicated in corruption should be put to jail instead of those who demand accountability and justice.


“Farmers, workers, journalists, doctors, human rights workers, and the marginalized sectors are arrested for serving the communities, those disadvantaged at most,” said Echanis in Filipino. “This is an important day for us to launch this nationwide and international campaign. The freedom of all political prisoners requires our collective action.”


Former political prisoner Amanda Echanis is the spokesperson of LAYA campaign network. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.


She added in a separate statement, “What has become clearer, especially amidst the hearings on the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, that those in power will do anything not to be held accountable, while the people are sickened by their waste of funds not only to steal from people’s money, but also to ensure that they go scot-free.”


The LAYA campaign aims to unite organizations and individuals, and appeal to those in government to facilitate the speedy release of political prisoners, especially those with humanitarian considerations, like the sick …

author: Susan Price
title: Malaysia: Protesting Australian rare earth mining company’s deal with the Pentagon
content:
Ever since Western Australian-based Lynas Rare Earths set up the world’s largest rare earth refinery outside of China near the Malaysian city of Kuantan, it has faced strong community opposition based on well-founded concerns about the plant’s radioactive waste.

A broader coalition held a protest outside Malaysia’s parliament in Kuala Lumpur, on July 6, focusing on the company’s possible complicity in Israel’s genocide in Gaza.

A parliamentary special select committee began reviewing Lynas’ role in the United States’ defence supply chain, on July 16.

Using a pseudonym, Mikhaal, from the Malaysian Protest 4 Palestine (MP4P) coalition told Green Left: “While there is no direct link between Lynas and the Israeli military, a March 16 binding letter of intent signed between Lynas and the US Department of War puts Lynas squarely in the supply chain of the US military.

“And since the US have been supplying the Israeli military with billions of dollars worth of military aid — more so during the past three years — there is strong reason to suspect that Lynas products may be used to aid the genocide in Gaza.

“[Anti-]Lynas protests for the past decade have mainly been focusing on environmental concerns, that the plant produces radioactive waste that is detrimental both to health and the environment, but now Lynas has also signed a deal with the US military, potentially leading to killing of innocents, wars and genocides.

“The alliance has expanded to include groups that are pro-Palestine, anti-imperialist, anti-war and anti-genocide.”

The protest demanded that Lynas cancel the agreement to sell US$96 million (A$137 million) worth of rare earth oxides to the Pentagon and suspend all rare earth exports to the Pentagon, pending an independent investigation to ensure the deal’s consistency with Malaysian policy and law.

MP4P also called for the full public disclosure of end-use agreements and military supply chain audits for Lynas’ rare earth exports over the past decade. It called on the government to suspend Lynas’ operations and revoke its operating license until the company cancels its Pentagon deal.

Further, MP4P called for legislation “prohibiting any future rare earth exports from Malaysia when there is credible risk that they will be used in violations of international humanitarian law, including genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity”.

It reiterated an earlier call by environmental groups for Lynas to strictly adhere to its original licensing condition to remove all radioactive water leach purification residue — a byproduct of rare earths processing — from Malaysia.

Protesters said any moves to expand Lynas’ operation in Malaysia should be blocked until the company properly adheres to its original licensing condition to protect public and environmental health.

They called on the government, which has been vociferous in its condemnation of Israel’s genocide in Gaza, to take “proactive diplomatic action through the UN Security Council and International Criminal Court to cut off other nations’ similar resources to Israel”.

“We have laid out the mechanism through which we can get the deal cancelled,” Mikhaal said.

“We have an Act that allows us to impose any condition as is necessary for any plant to be able to get their operating licence. So our suggestion in the parliamentary hearing is to include ‘not supplying rare earth to any foreign military’ as one of the conditions for their operating licence, and revoking their licence if Lynas can’t fulfil it.

“We hope that the government can take this course of action.”

Lynas has lucratively exploited Western military and strategic drives to reduce China’s dominant role in the production of rare earths and critical minerals.

Lee Tan, a policy coordinator and researcher with Aid Watch Australia who has been closely monitoring Lynas, told GL that the Pentagon has financed Lynas with more than US$350 million (A$500 million) in investment.

“In 2020, it awarded initial funding to Lynas and the Texas-based Blue Line Corporation for a heavy rare earths separation plant in Texas.

“Then in 2021, the Pentagon awarded Lynas a further US$30.4 million (A$43 million) to establish a commercial light rare earth separation facility in Hondo, Texas.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Anti-CFMEU campaign wedges Vic Labor in election year
content:
With Jacinta Allan’s Labor government polling third place in the Victorian election in November, the bosses are amping up their anti-union campaign, demanding she call a royal commission to uncover “hidden” evidence of unlawfulness in the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU).

The establishment media, including the ABC, is driving the campaign against the CFMEU. Nick McKenzie, from The Age, is leading the charge on the Victorian government’s failure to “clean up” the “industry”.

Almost every day, there is another attack piece.

On July 20, McKenzie and Kieran Rooney alleged that “Labor’s signature $100 billion Big Build program had been infiltrated by criminal gangs and corrupt union and business practices” and that Allan had failed to deal with the alleged problem. McKenzie and Rooney quote others in their salacious pieces, never verifying their sources.

The fact that no CFMEU official has been convicted in Victoria does not faze them.

The few charges that were laid against organisers, such as Gerry McCrudden or First Nations organiser Joel Shackleton, appear to have stalled, either due to lack of evidence or because they were so minor.

Predictably, Labor’s defence has been weak, because it too wants to weaken the CFMEU. It has supported and defended the federal Labor government’s forced administration of the CFMEU since August 2024.

The damage being done to Australia’s most militant, independent union may be irreversible.

Mark Irving, the former CFMEU administrator, laid out his restructure of the union in his third bi-annual report to the Minister for Employment and Workplace Relations in February, arguing the union would be made into a compliant union controlled by the Australian Council of Trade Unions (ACTU).

Many are only just beginning to understand the implications of Irving’s measures, which are being implemented by new CFMEU administrator Michael Crosby.

Since the mass outrage against the CFMEU takeover, there has been almost no fight-back. This is despite the entire leadership in Victoria, NSW, Queensland and South Australia being sacked. Irving sacked 90% of all coordinating staff and 90% of organisers in NSW, 60% in South Australia and 50% in Victoria and Queensland. There have been more sackings this year.

Irving boasted that it was a “regeneration of the staff”, implying that people chose to leave. But organisers were threatened with losing their entitlements or becoming “removed persons” — which would mean they would not be able to work for any other union if they did not resign from the CFMEU.

A series of ACTU officials with no construction industry experience, including Emma Kingdon and Matt McGowan, have been installed to run the CFMEU. (McGowan as National Tertiary Education Union general secretary unsuccessfully offered a 15% pay cut to the bosses in return for job security in 2020.)

Irving claimed this “team of professional executives” was required “to return the union to the democratic control of members as [a] principled, strong and independent union”.

However, there is no timeline for the CFMEU to be returned to the membership and there is no dialogue with members about the type of union they want. Victorian CFMEU members, who continue to meet monthly, are demanding answers from the CFMEU administration, but have received none.

Irving’s February report focused less on corruption allegations and more on the union’s supposed unlawful behaviour. He claimed that in the five years before 2024, the CFMEU had “engaged in 1163 contraventions of industrial laws” and developed “uncooperative relationships” with police, regulatory bodies and builders.

Irving claims that there has been no “unlawful behaviour” since the enforced administration, as the union is now based “more on co-operation and collaboration, and less on confrontation and conflict”.

Irving’s comments reveal that the federal government’s motivation for taking over the union is to control it — especially during the construction of the Olympic stadiums in Queensland and the AFL stadium in Lutruwita/Tasmania.

Labor governments and bosses want the flexibility to change rosters, or control days off, without fighting with the CFMEU, which has a militant record of fighting for the best and safest deals.

The rest of Irving’s report made clear that civil construction may be handed to the Australian Workers’ Union, which has a history of being more compliant.

author: Pip Hinman
title: Qld gov’t, bosses plan to hammer building workers
content:
Queensland’s Liberal National Party (LNP) government is proposing to cut construction workers’ pay and conditions and restrict their right to organise as part of its attack on the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU).

The proposals, which are part of the LNP’s bid to amend the state’s Building and Construction Code, go well beyond the limits already in place under federal industrial relations laws.

Unions counter that resourcing regulators of existing industrial relations, and health and safety laws, would resolve disputes in the building industry. But their ability to mobilise their members to protect their interests against the LNP and employers’ attacks is hamstrung by the federal government’s imposition of administrators on the construction division of the CFMEU. The administrators have taken power away from the union’s delegates and removed the elected officials.

The LNP commission was set up to investigate the construction division. However, it is impacting the building industry broadly.

It is proposing a new building and construction code to replace the former Labor government’s Best Practice Industry Conditions policy, which the LNP paused soon after being elected. It wants the new code in place before negotiations on enterprise agreements begin over infrastructure building for the 2032 Olympic Games and other major infrastructure projects.

The proposed code would cover state government-funded projects costing as little as $2 million, but its reach would extend to “related entities”, subcontractors and private contractors. It means that companies signing up to the code will be corralled into attacking union-won conditions to be able to show improved productivity and reduced costs.

Construction company owner online publication The Good Builder sums up the proposed code as “a rebuild of the Australian Building and Construction Commission [ABCC], at state level”. The commission document justifying its proposal largely relies on testimony from Nigel Hadgkiss and Wayne Jenkinson, former leading anti-union ABCC figures.

The purported productivity gains will come from further work intensification in this dangerous industry; the federal government body SafeWork Australia has recorded more than 300 deaths in the construction industry from 2015 to 2024.

A Queensland unionist told the commission of inquiry into the CFMEU that, where the union had an enterprise agreement on site, “it’s been over 17 years since there’s been a fatality”.

Reducing the power of the unions on the job, as the proposed code will do, will put the lives and limbs of building workers at even greater risk.

Should the LNP’s code be implemented, the changes would allow all-in pay arrangements, which tend to eliminate overtime and allowances.

• Limits to labour sources, opening up jobs to labour hire;

• Ratios for the employment of apprentices and trainees compared to other workers;

• “Last-on, first off” redundancy arrangements to allow employers to decide who to sack (including union activists).

Several measures in the proposed code directly attack union organising. It intends to ban payments linked to industrial action, such as “employ[ing] a non-working shop steward or job delegate”. This would limit the ability of a experienced senior delegate, or workplace health and safety representatives, to go on site with delegated time to perform their duties.

The code also proposes to restrict union training and a union’s right of entry to workplaces to the bare minimum as required in federal law. This means that only current delegates in companies with more than 15 employees will be able to have union training and union officials will struggle to get on to building sites.

The code would also require employers to clarify union coverage for sites. This is undoubtedly aimed to restrict the construction division’s coverage in favour of the historically less militant Australian Workers’ Union.

2010 call for international noise demos

An excerpt from: For a new combat position of anarchist insurgency-For a Black December

Notes on the practice of prison noise demos in South-western Ontario 2008–2015

“The prison door opens, and now he knows what to do; keep the memory alive, leave no space for oblivion, never forget the comrades left behind, pick up the thread of insurgency from where it was interrupted, pour the poison of insubordination into the reproduction networks of the capitalist society”

From “For a new combat position of anarchist insurgency – For a Black December”; by imprisonned anarchists Nikos Romanos and Panagiotous Argirou

For the past seven years, anarchist and other radicals in South-western Ontario have celebrated New Year’s Eve with noise demos outside of the areas many prisons. We love to party and celebrate on New Year’s and this tradition has allowed us to do so in a spirit of antagonism and solidarity. We can have fun in a way that actually inspires us and that brings some joy to people who are locked up.

Connecting through the walls with prisoners is a direct action against the alienation and separation that prison creates and it transforms the urban space, bringing in to focus the prisons that dot the landscape and making vivid the coercive violence of the state that controls our lives. Prison impacts us every day, whether or not we’re locked up, and the New Year’s Noise Demos make this conflict tangible.

One of the initial intentions of the noise demos in Hamilton was to participate in an international practice of anarchist solidarity with prisoners. In 2009, it was a direct response to a call to support an international hunger strike campaign by anarchist prisoners, launched by Gabriel Pombo Da Silva from a prison in Germany.

The following year, several of our comrades were still locked up from the G20 mobilizations and there had been demos earlier in the year at Vanier/Maplehurst and The Don Jail in support of anarchist and other prisoners held there. This marked a time when, for many of us, the reality of prison intruded more starkly into our lives and the combative anger of the demos that year showed an escalation in hostility still anchored in the spirit of international solidarity, particularly with prisoners in the US state of Georgia who were on hunger strike and with an international call for new year’s noise demos (the exact same text has been re-released this year as a fresh call for demos).

This year, let’s show our solidarity with the international call for a Black December released by anarchist prisoners in Greece, Nikos Romanos and Panagiotis Argirou. They called for insurrectionary actions around the world which they hope “will be the detonator for the restart of anarchist insurgency, inside and outside the prisons”. Their call has already been answered by more than fifty actions around the world, including in Canada, where an attack on a police vehicle and a confrontational march in Montreal have been claimed as part of Black December. (There is a timeline of actions at rabble.org.uk).

From 2011, the demos expanded – to support prisoners in struggle at the Grand Valley Prison in Kitchener, to visit anarchist prisoners in West Toronto and in Penetanguishene, the Syl Apps youth prison in Oakville – while continuing to anchor themselves with a stop at Hamilton’s Barton Jail. This prison, described as a monument to human misery’, that looms over one of Canada’s poorest urban areas, remains very overcrowded and kills several of its prisoners every year.

The shit-eating screws of the OPSEU union use the Barton Jail as a centre-piece in their disputes with the province, allowing conditions there to degenerate to deadly levels to improve their negotiating position. In 2012, a so-called “strike” action by the guards only ended after a prisoner died following a month of lockdown. (But can they really be thought of as workers when their job is to manage the misery of others? Would not such an action more accurately be called hostage-taking or extortion?)

This year, we’re stopping at the new Toronto South, or Mimico, prison on the Toronto-Mississauga border. This new maximum security nightmare, which, when full, will be among the largest prisons in Canada, has already seen at least two prisoners die in the year it’s been open. Prisoners there …

author: Agency
title: Press Release: Recently Unsealed Trial Evidence Contradicts Government’s Account of Events During Fourth of July Prairieland Noise Protest
content:
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE:

 July 20, 2026


Recently Unsealed Trial Evidence Contradicts Government’s Account of Events During Fourth of July Prairieland Noise Protest


DFW Support Committee Highlights Key Video Footage for Public, Which Federal Judge Mark Pittman Kept Under Seal for Weeks After Trial


FORT WORTH, TX

 — Four months after the federal Prairieland verdicts, and a year after the Fourth of July noise demonstration held in solidarity with ICE Detention Center detainees, around which the Prairieland case revolves, the DFW Support Committee was able to piece together trial evidence to debunk government claims and refute rampant mischaracterizations in the media of that night’s events.


The US District Court for the Northern District of Texas, which recently sentenced nine federal trial defendants to consecutive terms of 30-100 years in prison, kept key evidence sealed for weeks after the March trial had concluded. Until now, this evidence has not been widely viewed by the public. The DFW Support Committee has highlighted certain video evidence that shows the July 4 demonstration was not an ambush or an attack—the dominant narrative coming from the government and uncritically repeated by mainstream media. CCTV footage depicts a largely uneventful gathering aside from a few protesters shooting fireworks into the air and minor vandalism. The evidence also shows a police officer arriving on the scene, quickly drawing his firearm, aiming it at departing protesters, and firing, despite the clear absence of any threat.


The government’s charges of using and carrying explosives, as well as conspiracy to do so, stem from the use of consumer grade fireworks. Two different CCTV cameras (

GX13

 and

GX14

) recorded footage of fireworks being shot into the air, not at the detention facility, as some news media claim. The same footage shows protesters leaving when asked to do so by detention center staff. Additional CCTV footage (

GX11

) shows minor vandalism, including spray painting a police vehicle, carried out by a single individual. Instead of charging that person with vandalism, the government dubbed the protest a riot and charged eight defendants with rioting and material support for terrorism for the same minor vandalism carried out by a single person. 


After the noise, fireworks, and minor vandalism took place the night of July 4, 2025, the scene at the Prairieland ICE Detention Center—a razor wire, fully-fenced fortress—was relatively calm. It was only after Alvarado Police Department Lt. Thomas Gross arrived on the scene that things escalated.


Bodycam footage from Lt. Gross (

GX3

) shows him exiting his vehicle and immediately pointing his gun at the back of a protester, before taking a shooting stance and firing. Additional CCTV footage from the detention facility (

GX10 at 1:29:26

) shows a protester running away, Lt. Gross aiming at them, and Prairieland defendant Benjamin “Champagne” Song firing suppressive shots at the ground to avert the murder of the fleeing protester. Rather than attempting to murder Lt. Gross, as the government claims, it appears clear that Song was trying to save a life. The events that this evidence depicts have been corroborated by Song in a

post-sentencing statement

. But when Song’s lawyers attempted to argue “defense of another” at trial, the government filed an

emergency motion

 to block the argument. In a ruling that contradicted his own timeliness rules for motions and arguably outside of his authority, US District Court Judge Mark Pittman granted the government’s motion.


Moreover, bodycam footage from Lt. Gross (

GX3 at 2:23

) reveals that the projectile trails emerging from Song’s direction are angled away from the officer in an entirely different direction, making it implausible that a bullet from Song’s gun was what injured Lt. Gross. The same bodycam footage also shows that the projectile trail from Lt. Gross leaves his gun and returns virtually along the same path, indicating that his bullet may have ricocheted, which is not uncommon. Damage to Song’s rifle, which seems to indicate that a bullet hit it, supports a scenario in which Lt. Gross’s bullet ricocheted off of Song’s rifle to graze Lt. Gross on its return. In addition, the photographic evidence of his impact wound (

GX4, page 4

) does not fit the profile of a direct hit from the kind of semi-automatic rifle used by Song, but does fit the kind of injury sustained from a ricocheted bullet …

author: Andrés
title: Palta & The Mood hizo de Niceto una pista de baile y celebración colectiva
content:
Foto: Daniel Ávalos


Con un Niceto Club colmado, Palta & The Mood volvió a confirmar por qué es una de las propuestas más sólidas de la escena independiente argentina. El recital del viernes 17 de julio fue mucho más que la presentación de un repertorio: se transformó en una celebración compartida donde el funk, el soul y el R&B encontraron su mejor expresión en el ida y vuelta permanente con el público. Por Daniel Ávalos para

ANRed

.


Foto: Daniel Ávalos


Desde los primeros temas, la banda desplegó un sonido preciso y potente. La sección rítmica sostuvo un groove constante, mientras los vientos y los teclados construyeron una atmósfera que invitó al movimiento. Lejos de un show pensado únicamente para la contemplación, la propuesta buscó romper la distancia entre escenario y platea, convirtiendo a Niceto en una gran pista de baile.


El recorrido por su repertorio combinó canciones ya consolidadas con material más reciente, mostrando la evolución de un grupo que continúa ampliando su identidad sin perder la esencia. La respuesta del público fue inmediata. Cuerpos en movimiento acompañaron cada canción en un clima festivo que se sostuvo durante toda la noche. Esa conexión, construida recital tras recital, explica buena parte del crecimiento de Palta & The Mood dentro del circuito musical argentino.


Foto: Daniel Ávalos


En tiempos donde buena parte de la escena independiente enfrenta dificultades para sostener espacios de circulación, propuestas como la de Palta & The Mood demuestran que existe un público dispuesto a acompañar proyectos que privilegian la calidad artística, el trabajo colectivo y la experiencia del vivo. El show en Niceto no fue solamente un concierto: fue la confirmación de una banda que sigue consolidando un lugar propio, y de una comunidad que hace de la música un espacio de encuentro.

author: Yasmine Johnson
title: A Jewish socialist responds to the Murdoch press
content:
Last week, I appeared at the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion to defend the Palestine solidarity movement against the slanders of the Australian political establishment and an organised and ideologically hardened bloc of pro-Israel students and staff.

I did so because our movement has been the only decent human response to the barbarism being carried out by Israel in Gaza. I wanted to defend the 300,000 people who marched across the Sydney Harbour Bridge, the tens of thousands of students who rallied, camped and organised on campuses around the country, and the millions internationally who have refused to stay silent while Palestinians endure genocide.

During the commission, witnesses—almost invariably supporters of Israel—have downplayed the scale of death in Gaza, suggested that Palestinian flags, keffiyehs and even Arabic script constitute antisemitism, and repeatedly blurred distinctions between Jewish identity, political Zionism and the actions of the Israeli state. 

The

Herald Sun

 and the

Australian

 newspapers, among others, have uncritically reported the testimonies of the pro-Israel bloc, while repeating their lies and slanders against the anti-war movement. They have also distorted the incredibly limited testimony challenging the slanders.

According to a

Herald Sun

headline

, for example, I described the “murder of Israelis” as “acts of mass resistance”. It’s a remarkable distortion. What I said was something very different, and historically obvious: people living under colonial rule and other forms of oppressive tyranny, and facing the sort of mass destruction we see in Palestine, have invariably resisted in many different ways. Some movements have relied primarily on strikes, protests and civil disobedience. Many have also included armed resistance. 

So I stand by the quote that the

Australian

 presented as a scandal: “I refuse to hold movements for the justice of the oppressed to a standard that says there can never be any violence”.

Were the Jews who were forced into the Warsaw Ghetto wrong to resist the Nazis by whatever means they had at their disposal? I say they were right to resist. The

Herald Sun

 and

Australian

 editorialists, by contrast, would probably have denounced resistance leader Marek Edelman and his comrades as a bloodthirsty, human-shield using terrorists on reading

his testimony of killing German soldiers

 and proudly declaring that “German blood flooded the street” in Warsaw. Take the following recollection as indicative of the mindset of the ghetto partisans:

“Now something unprecedented took place. Three [German] officers with lowered machine pistols appeared. They wore white rosettes in their buttonholes-emissaries. They desired to negotiate with the Area Command. They proposed a 15-minute truce to remove the dead and the wounded ... Firing was our answer. Every house remained a hostile fortress. From every storey, from every window bullets sought hated German helmets, hated German hearts.”

Was it not right for Indians to fight against British colonial rule? Does the fact that they used armed resistance invalidate the justice of their cause? Karl Marx,

in an 1857

New York Daily Tribune

 article about the Lucknow uprising, noted that the “outrages committed by the revolted Sepoys in India [sepoys were Indian soldiers recruited to the British military] are indeed appalling, hideous, ineffable”. But he went on to say that the conduct of the uprising was of the sort that “respectable England used to applaud” when carried out by the forces it supported. He continued:

“However infamous the conduct of the Sepoys, it is only the reflex, in a concentrated form, of England’s own conduct in India, not only during the epoch of the foundation of her Eastern Empire, but even during the last ten years of a long-settled rule. To characterize that rule, it suffices to say that torture formed an organic institution of its financial policy. There is something in human history like retribution: and it is a rule of historical retribution that its instrument be forged not by the offended, but by the offender himself.”

Well may we apply this observation to Israel and Palestine, where Zionist barbarity over decades has produced, on a remarkably small number of occassions given the sustained assault the Palestinians have endured since 1948, a reflex aimed at retribution.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Presos políticos: crece la campaña por la libertad de Milton y Eneas
content:
El pasado sábado 18 de julio en el Espacio de Memoria CCD “El Infierno”, en Avellaneda, se dieron cita casi cien activistas representantes de una treintena de organizaciones políticas, organismos de DDHH, asambleas barriales, cooperativas y movimientos sociales para debatir en plenario qué acciones seguir por la libertad de los presos de las luchas contra la reforma laboral.


Por corresponsal popular: Comisión Vecinxs Justicia por Campomar en el Encuentro Memoria Verdad y Justicia

@xlacomisaria3ra

. Fotos:

ioruelcam


@sofiasaluzzisoy


La jornada abrió con la presentación de la Coordinadora por lxs Presxs Políticxs (

@coordi.presxspoliticxs

) a les presentes. La misma es heredera de aquella que organizara el acompañamiento a lxs presxs de La Ley Bases a instancias del Encuentro Memoria Verdad y Justicia. Viene sosteniendo tareas de cuidado y propaganda desde sus comisiones de acopio de mercadería y visitas, prensa, agitación y movilización, finanzas y jurídica; así como a partir de la organización de festivales en diferentes puntos del conurbano.


Desde este espacio se valoró emotivamente la apertura del Espacio de Memoria a una lucha actual, homenajeando a les compañeres que pasaron por ese Centro Clandestino que presidían simbólicamente el evento. Después de todo, se recordaron las evidentes continuidades entre la política dictatorial contra que luchaban les 30.400 con las de la derecha argentina y mundial en la actualidad.


Se abrió vitoreando la buena noticia que no se espera una nueva detención de Homero, procesado en la misma causa que Milton y Eneas. Y a continuación se escucharon los audios de ambos compañeros desde el penal de Marcos Paz agradeciendo el acompañamiento y arengando a seguir la lucha social contra este gobierno. Intervino también Eduardo Castellanos, ex detenido del Infierno y declarante en varios juicios de lesa humanidad quien usó su espacio para contar los avances del juicio a la CNU en La Plata.


Luego del recibimiento por el subsecretario de DDHH de Avellaneda, Jorge García; y de una rápida visita guiada por el lugar, les participantes se dividieron en cinco comisiones de trabajo.


Las discusiones fueron en todos los grupos sobre los desafíos del proceso de criminalización de la protesta por parte de este gobierno y la búsqueda de ideas para hacer avanzar la campaña por la libertad de Milton y Eneas.


De la puesta en común salieron variedad propuestas para romper el cerco mediático, pensando acciones de visibilización con consignas que no requieran un alto nivel de politización para generar sensibilidad. Se debatió la manera de romper los algoritmos tanto por el lado de la coordinación en la virtualidad como por una “vuelta” a la intervención física (carteles, pintadas, pasacalles, stickers) que permita redirigir a las redes de la Coordinadora a personas ajenas a la problemática.


Así mismo, se reafirmó la necesidad que todes les presentes se apropien de la campaña llevándola a todos los conflictos, acciones y espacios de militancia con las herramientas que produce la coordinadora o con su propia impronta.


Se reafirmó la intención del espacio de lanzar una campaña audiovisual, una gran campaña de firmas y una movilización hacia el 19 de agosto. En general se coincidió en la centralidad en términos de solidaridad de clase que implica la libertad de lxs presxs políticos y los múltiples vasos comunicantes que vinculan cada conflicto popular con las luchas en Congreso por la reforma laboral por las que se procesa a Milton y Eneas.


A instancias de este plenario, se incorporaron activistas de varios espacios al funcionamiento de la Coordinadora.


El encuentro cerró con un audio del Secretario de DDHH de Avellaneda Claudio Yacoy disculpándose por su ausencia, unas palabras del diputado del PJ CABA Andrés La Blunda y el saludo agradecido de Fabian Grillo, papá de Pablo al activismo allí presente. Luego el dúo La García Barrios (

@musicalagarcia

) cantó apasionadamente algunos temas de Silvio Rodríguez segundeades por varies de los presentes.
